lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. On which day in 1948 was it agreed? (10 December.) Today: the United Nations, the Declaration's story, and the people who fought for civil rights.

After the Second World War, countries wanted such horrors never to happen again. In 1945 they founded the United Nations, to keep the peace, help countries work together and protect human rights. Its peacekeepers wear blue helmets.

On 10 December 1948 the UN agreed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: 30 articles for everyone, everywhere. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the writing, with René Cassin, P. C. Chang and others; Hansa Mehta of India made 'all men' into 'all human beings'.

Article 1 says all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Others include life and liberty (3), no slavery (4) and equality before the law (7). Belief (18), free speech (19), work (23) and education (26) are there too.

In the USA, many Black Americans were kept apart by law (segregation) and stopped from voting. Rosa Parks's protest began the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955; in 1963 Martin Luther King Jr spoke of his dream in Washington. Laws in 1964-65 ended it.

In Britain, the Windrush generation came from the Caribbean from 1948 to help rebuild. In 1963 a Bristol bus company refused to hire Black drivers; a boycott led by Paul Stephenson changed that. The Race Relations Act of 1965 made some discrimination illegal.

In South Africa, apartheid (1948-1994) separated people by race in law. Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for 27 years for opposing it. People in South Africa and around the world campaigned; in 1994 everyone could vote, and Mandela became president.

Try it in the world: read Henry Dunant's story in Success Stories, on the Story Shelf: how the Red Cross began. Then make a rights wall in your village: five articles in your own words. Next: the space race and the digital age.

exercises.prompt: In which year did the UN agree the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
exercises.hint: It was three years after the UN was founded in 1945.
exercises.explain: On 10 December 1948, now Human Rights Day.

exercises.prompt: Who chaired the writing of the Universal Declaration?
exercises.hint: She had been the First Lady of the USA.
exercises.explain: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the committee that wrote it.

exercises.hint: Look back at the card about the Declaration.
exercises.explain: True: 30 articles of rights for everyone, everywhere.

choices: separating people by race in law
exercises.explain: South Africa's system, 1948-1994, that separated people by race and denied most of them rights.

exercises.prompt: Match each person to their struggle.
exercises.hint: Two bus boycotts, a march and a long struggle in South Africa.
exercises.explain: Rosa Parks: Montgomery. Martin Luther King Jr: Washington. Paul Stephenson: Bristol. Nelson Mandela: apartheid.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
Sort these: civil rights in the USA, or in Britain?
exercises.hint: Montgomery and Washington are in the USA; Bristol is in England.
exercises.explain: The USA: Montgomery, Washington, the Voting Rights Act. Britain: Bristol, Windrush, the Race Relations Act.

exercises.prompt: Apartheid lasted from 1948 to 1994. For how many years was that?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.

exercises.prompt: What does Article 1 of the Declaration say?
choices: all human beings are born free and equal
exercises.hint: It is the first and widest promise.
exercises.explain: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

exercises.prompt: Hansa Mehta changed 'all men' to 'all human beings' in Article 1.
exercises.hint: Think of who 'all men' might seem to leave out.
exercises.explain: True: thanks to her, the first article clearly includes women and men alike.

exercises.prompt: Why did the UN write a declaration of human rights in 1948?
choices: so the war's horrors never happen again
so one country rules the world
exercises.hint: Think of what the world had just seen in the war and the Holocaust.
exercises.explain: After the war and the Holocaust, countries promised rights for everyone, to stop such horrors happening again.

exercises.prompt: Why was the Montgomery bus boycott so powerful?
choices: the bus company lost money and the world watched
exercises.hint: Think about who loses when thousands stop paying for something.
exercises.explain: For 381 days Black passengers refused the buses; the company lost fares, the world watched, and the courts ended bus segregation.

exercises.prompt: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days. How many whole weeks is that?
exercises.hint: Divide by 7 and leave out the days over.
exercises.explain: 7 × 54 = 378, and 381 − 378 = 3, so 54 whole weeks and 3 days.

exercises.prompt: New laws alone ended racism in the USA, Britain and South Africa.
exercises.hint: Ask whether changing a law changes every person's mind.
exercises.explain: False: laws were a big step, but prejudice did not vanish; people still work for fairness today.

exercises.prompt: The Declaration was agreed in 1948. How many years old was it in 2023?
exercises.hint: Take the earlier year from the later one.
